title: Al-Hakam, the Judge
hookLine: the Judge, whose judgment is final
tomorrow: fair, even against your own family? one verse says yes.

lines: A MAN THEY CALLED THE JUDGE.
cards: A stranger posts one blurry paragraph about a fight with her sister, asking: was I wrong? Underneath, hundreds of verdicts from people who will never meet either of them. Handing out verdicts feels good.

It feels a little like power. A man in Arabia had that power for real. His people brought him their disputes, and both sides left content, so they gave him a proud nickname: Abu al-Hakam, father of the judge.
Yesterday's question was why the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, changed it. Here's what happened when they met.

teach.b: The Prophet heard the nickname and said: Allah is al-Hakam, and judgment belongs to Him, so why are you called that? The man explained. When my people disagree, I judge between them, and both sides are satisfied.
And the Prophet said: how good this is. Notice that. The peacemaking wasn't the problem.
Then he asked about the man's children, heard that the eldest was Shurayh, and said: then you are Abu Shurayh. A father's name, after his son. The work stayed.
The title went back to its owner. That's today's Name. Al-Hakam, the Judge.
People still settle disputes, run courts, call a foul a foul. But the last word on a person, on what's inside them and where they end up, isn't ours to hold.
The Qur'an asks it as a question, in Surah at-Tin: "Is not Allah the most conclusive of all judges?"
Here's the line to tell a friend tonight: in this hadith, a man who settled fights well got a new name, after his kid. One verdict to set down, today, could be the one about someone you barely know.

how: Muslims settle disputes through judges, arbiters and family elders, while holding that final judgment of a person belongs to Allah; Surah at-Tin closes by asking whether Allah is not the most conclusive of judges.

o: the one who judges only on the last day
the Judge, whose ruling is the final one
the one who forbids every human court

games.q: the man and his name — tap the pairs.
p: the nickname: father of the judge
the new name, after his eldest son
what the Prophet said of his peacemaking
the most conclusive of all judges

s: leaving judgment to God means you can never call anything wrong
the man settled disputes, and the Prophet praised it: how good this is.
the man lost his nickname because he was a bad judge
his judging pleased both sides. the title 'the judge' belonged to Allah.
his new name came from his son, Shurayh
a father's name, after his eldest: Abu Shurayh.

games.q: you saw a teammate copy answers on a quiz. your friends want your verdict: is she just a bad person? what fits Al-Hakam?
o: tell the teacher if it matters, and leave the verdict on her as a person to God.
say yes, she's a cheater; facts are facts and people should know.
say nothing to anyone, ever; only God can judge anything at all.
games.why: a foul can be called a foul; the man who judged disputes was praised. what goes back to Allah is the last word on who she is.

practice: Pick up something small in each hand: a pen, a coin, a key. Feel the two weights. Let one of them stand for a verdict you've been carrying about someone this week.
Set that one down on the table, let go of it, and leave it there for the sit.

wordCard.voice: Al-Hakam. The Judge, whose judgment is final, and whose title a good peacemaker gave back.

orig.note: Arabic: the Judge, the one whose ruling is final. the title the Prophet said belongs to Allah.

carryVoice: Hold on to this: he judges, so the last word on a person is never yours to carry. Go gently.

sources.q: Is not Allah the most conclusive of all judges?
